title.en: Is the soil a gift or an asset?

text.en: A farmer in Punjab and a miner in Jharkhand both depend on the earth. But a handful of soil is useful only when people know how to use it. That is the big idea of this chapter: nature gives materials, human beings turn them into resources.

The textbook says that everything in our environment that can satisfy our needs is a resource, provided it is technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable.
Resources are not just free gifts of nature. Human beings transform materials into resources through technology and create institutions to speed up development.
Resources are classified in four ways: by origin as biotic and abiotic, by exhaustibility as renewable and non-renewable, by ownership as individual, community, national and international, and by status of development as potential, developed, stock and reserves.
Careless use of resources causes depletion, divides society into haves and have-nots, and leads to global warming, ozone depletion and land degradation. So we need sustainable development, meaning development that does not compromise the needs of future generations.
The Rio de Janeiro Earth Summit of 1992 adopted Agenda 21, which asks every local government to draw up its own local Agenda 21.
Resource planning is a three-step process: identify and inventory resources, evolve a planning structure with technology and institutions, and match the plan with national development plans.
Land is used for forests, land not available for cultivation, other uncultivated land, fallow land and net sown area. Soils in India are alluvial, black, red and yellow, laterite, arid and forest soils.
Land degradation is checked by afforestation, proper grazing, shelter belts, stabilising sand dunes with thorny bushes and controlling mining and industrial waste.

problem.en: A state has 40 per cent of its area as net sown area and 20 per cent as forest. What per cent is left for all other uses?

text.en: Add the two given shares: 40 + 20 = 60 per cent.
Subtract from the whole: 100 - 60 = 40 per cent.

why.en: The rest is fallow, uncultivated and non-agricultural use.

prompt.en: Explain why a resource is more than a free gift of nature.

requiredIdeas.en: Resource needs technology, economy and culture to be usable
Sustainable use keeps resources for the future

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking all materials in nature are resources by themselves

points.en: Resources depend on technology, economic feasibility and cultural acceptance.
They are classified by origin, exhaustibility, ownership and status of development.
Sustainable development protects the needs of future generations.
India has six main soil types and five main land-use categories.
